idiom_name: immutable class with const members and `std::tie`/memberwise `operator==`
implementation_notes: C++ already gives value semantics: copy construction and assignment, `const` members and operator overloading mean a small class becomes a value object as soon as its state is immutable and `operator==` is defined memberwise (or via `std::tie` comparison). The hand-written operators are the pre-C++20 route and remain justified on older toolchains, in code that must stay compilable as C++11/14/17, and wherever comparison needs semantics the compiler cannot derive (case-insensitive codes, tolerances). Keep members private and return by value or const reference; a mutating setter belongs on a new instance.
pitfalls: `operator==` must be consistent with the hasher used in `std::unordered_set`/`std::unordered_map`, otherwise equal values land in different buckets and lookups silently fail.
Exposing non-const accessors or `mutable` members reopens the aliasing bug the pattern removes.
A user-declared destructor or copy operation suppresses implicit move operations and forces copies - follow the rule of zero, or declare all five operations deliberately.

variants.name: C++20 defaulted comparison
variants.implementation_notes: On C++20 the compiler synthesises memberwise `operator==` and `operator<=>` from one defaulted declaration, so the value class carries no hand-written comparison code; a defaulted `<=>` also implicitly declares `operator==`, and the comparison is deleted when a member is not comparable. Prefer this variant wherever the toolchain is C++20 or newer; keep the classic hand-written form when only part of the state should participate in equality (defaulted comparison always uses all subobjects) or when the standard floor is lower.
pitfalls: A hand-written `<=>` does not synthesise `operator==` - declare `bool operator==(const Quantity&) const = default;` explicitly when ordering is customised.
Defaulted comparison covers every subobject in declaration order, so a cache or derived member silently joins equality; move such state out of the class or write the comparison by hand.
Floating-point members make the defaulted `<=>` a `partial_ordering` and keep IEEE equality semantics (NaN != NaN), which may not be the domain's equality.
